title: Chapter 3 — Individualism Stronger At The Close Of A Democratic Revolution Than At Other Periods
paragraphs: The time when the building of a democratic society on the ruins of an aristocracy has just been completed is the time when this separation of men from one another, and the egotism that results from it, most forcibly strike the observer. Democratic communities contain not only a large number of independent citizens. They are also constantly filled with men who entered their independent condition only yesterday and are intoxicated with their new power. These men have a presumptuous confidence in their strength. They do not suppose that they will ever again need to ask their fellow creatures for help, so they do not hesitate to show that they care for nobody but themselves.

An aristocracy seldom yields without a long struggle, in the course of which implacable hatreds are kindled between the different classes of society. These passions outlast the victory, and traces of them can be seen in the democratic confusion that follows. Those members of the community who were at the top of the old gradations of rank cannot immediately forget their former greatness. For a long time they will regard themselves as strangers in the newly formed society. They look upon all those whom this state of society has made their equals as oppressors, whose fate can arouse no sympathy. They have lost sight of their former equals and no longer feel bound to their fate by any common interest. Each of them, standing apart, thinks he is reduced to caring for himself alone. Those who were formerly at the foot of the social scale, and who have been brought up to the common level by a sudden revolution, cannot enjoy their newly acquired independence without a secret uneasiness. If they meet some of their former superiors on the same footing as themselves, they keep away from them with an air of triumph and of fear. It is therefore usually at the outset of democratic society that citizens are most inclined to live apart. Democracy does not lead men to draw closer to their fellow creatures, but democratic revolutions lead them to avoid one another, and to carry into a state of equality the hatreds that the state of inequality produced. The great advantage of the Americans is that they have arrived at a state of democracy without having to go through a democratic revolution, and that they are born equal instead of becoming so.
